(Although I would say the wins were bigger for the Greens who got massive concessions out of the government on the digital duty of care, trusts, and private health insurance bills.) We are facing at the next election clearly a Coalition and Liberals and One Nation with all the baggage that each of these parties brings to the table. item.title: High levels of salmonella found in some products from nation’s biggest turkey producer
item.description: Two years of inspections at four Butterball plants show rates far exceeding US averages in ground or chopped meat Inspectors found salmonella bacteria in more than a third of ground or chopped turkey samples at slaughterhouses owned by Butterball, the US’s biggest turkey company, data shows. The US Department of Agriculture’s (USDA) food safety and inspection service (FSIS) and some states conduct regular checks for salmonella and other bacteria in commercial poultry plants. Salmonella can live in the intestines of poultry, and it can cause nausea, diarrhea and even death in humans if meat is not cooked properly and then consumed. Continue reading...

Chip Wilson, who built the Vancouver yoga-wear startup into a global athleisure empire, was a featured speaker at the Leadership Forum in Calgary earlier this week, an event organized by Axis Connects to advance women in leadership. item.title: Wisconsin rail tunnel dug from both ends with 1-inch error reopens after 7 years
item.description: The Stewart Tunnel in Wisconsin has officially reopened for cyclists after an extensive restoration initiative. It was closed in 2019 due to safety hazards associated with falling rocks, prompting significant renovation work. Originally constructed in 1886 for the Illinois Central Railroad, the tunnel historically facilitated passenger and freight transport until the 1970s. The restoration included adding a metal liner and drainage to enhance safety while maintaining its historic character.

item.title: The Guardian view on the next UN secretary general: sacrificing principles will damn the institution, not save it | Editorial
item.description: The UK must continue to oppose the UAE’s tainted nominee, Lana Nusseibeh. The ethical course is also the pragmatic one The future of the United Nations has rarely looked more perilous in an age of impunity for atrocities, raging wars, open US hostility, a funding crisis and security council deadlock. It is widely agreed that the choice of its next secretary general is critical – perhaps even existential. Unfortunately, that’s where agreement ends. Under the opaque selection system, security council members are privately polled on their views of each candidate. A “discourage” vote from one of the five permanent members is diplomacy-speak for a veto. Only when a consensus emerges does the general assembly get a say on the candidate. The next straw poll is due on Monday, with no deal yet in sight . With António Guterres completing his term on 31 December, the seat could fall empty for the first time. Continue reading...

item.title: Gukesh and Sindarov draw Game 2 of world chess championship in just 20 moves
item.description: Game 2 ends by threefold repetition in 1hr 57min World champion opens with the London System Sindarov plays with white in Game 3 on Thursday All your Gukesh v Sindarov questions, answered India’s Gukesh Dommaraju and Uzbekistan’s Javokhir Sindarov drew the second game of their world chess championship match in only 20 moves and 1hr 57min on Wednesday, leaving the score level at 1–all at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in the Geneva suburbs. The quiet encounter was one of the shortest classical world title games since the sport’s rival championships were reunified in 2006 and the first to finish in under two hours since Ding Liren and Ian Nepomniachtchi drew their 11th game in just over 100 minutes in Astana in 2023. item.description: Arsenal midfielder capped by England 19 times whose life after football suffered a drink-fuelled decline The footballer Peter Storey , who has died aged 81, was a tough-tackling midfielder for Arsenal when they won the double of the First Division championship and the FA Cup in 1971. Arsenal were only the fourth team to achieve the double at that point (it has since been won another nine times), and Storey, who appeared in 49 of the 51 league and FA Cup games that season, played as big a role as anyone in securing the honours with his defensive solidity, ball-winning skills, “good engine”, sound distribution and reliable occasional penalty taking. item.title: Is Vanity Fair’s takedown of Taylor Swift illuminating – or just a lot of hot air? | Arwa Mahdawi
item.description: A war correspondent interviewed 100 sources about the pop star, but what does the 4,500-word story reveal? If you are extremely online you will have known for a while that a big takedown was coming. An exposé of a well-known blond billionaire, a powerful figure that people are terrified to criticise, was in the works at a large publication. A former war correspondent had been assigned the story! A hundred sources had been interviewed! The reporting had taken a year! The truth would finally out! For everyone else, let me explain in plain English. On Monday Vanity Fair published an eagerly anticipated, 4,500-word piece, about Taylor Swift called The Mastermind. While it was labelled as “commentary”, it was framed as a deeply sourced piece written by May Jeong, a journalism professor at Princeton who has won awards for her reporting from Afghanistan. item.title: They belong to Jerusalem’s past and present: meet the African Palestinians
item.description: Despite militarisation, occupation and marginalisation, African culture prevails in the Old City, something I discovered first-hand when I visited Don’t get The Long Wave delivered to your inbox? Sign up here In occupied East Jerusalem, I met an often overlooked community: African Palestinians. This week, I explore their unique history, and how they are, in a classic diaspora fashion, integrated and marginalised in equal measure. There are about 450 African Palestinian people in occupied East Jerusalem, mostly living in the historical buildings of the Old City, near al-Aqsa mosque. That mosque, the third holiest site in Islam after those in Mecca and Medina, is the reason they are there. item.title: Bill Bailey is an absolute master of musical mischief – this crowd hangs on every twang
item.description: SEC Armadillo, Glasgow The comedian’s new concoction, Vaudevillean, mixes offbeat historical diversions, topical gags and virtuoso musical flights with warmth and absurdity Is any act ever really too niche for stardom? What could be more leftfield, after all, than Bill Bailey’s animated pop-musicology, with demonstrations on the Swedish nyckelharpa and the one-stringed Indian lute? But tonight he has yet another arena crowd hanging on his every strum, drumbeat and twang. Nothing need be niche, perhaps, if communicated with the open-hearted curiosity and passion Bailey brings to his esoteric interests. Add a flair for improbable juxtaposition, and a sense of humour that dusts curmudgeonliness with surrealism, and you’ve got a concoction that thousands-strong audiences find difficult to resist. He then became a very successful movie star in India. They had a remarkable, unusual life . I thought it was normal. In 1970, my parents decided to take a family holiday in Panjim in Goa. We stayed at the Mandovi hotel, an amazing place. I remember it vividly. item.title: Premier League’s burst of early sendings-off may not last – but red cards are on the rise for a reason
item.description: While referees tend to reach for red early in the season before easing off, players are under increasing pressure to keep pace in a frenetic environment Off! Off! Off! Brighton’s Costinha was sent off for two bookings at Hull, Leny Yoro collected a red card against Liverpool for denying a goalscoring opportunity ( though his suspension was overturned on appeal) and James Tarkowski saw red for serious foul play at Brentford. This season is shaping up to be an outlier in the VAR era of officiating in English football. The latest red cards took the Premier League total to 22 in 2026-27. The rate of 0.2 per game equates to 76 across the whole season, which would equal the Premier League record set in 2005-06. Refereeing has evolved in the past decade, though. My older brother Abdullah had taught it to me when I was nine: lie down on a speed bump, legs long and both arms outstretched by your ears, making your body a long pencil. I was in the wrong position that day – it was so hot that the backs of my shins seared when they touched the road, so I had to bend my knees. item.description: DuVernay’s follow-up to her dissection of the 13th Amendment to the US constitution is a vehement and exhilarating defence of democracy Ava DuVernay’s previous documentary 13th , energised by the Black Lives Matter movement, was a brilliant polemic about the 13th Amendment to the US constitution , which she argued perpetuated a link between slavery and prison for African American men. She's interviewed rock stars, changed the conversation around feminism and written some of the funniest observations about modern life. She reveals what it was like growing up as the eldest of eight children in a home-schooled, unconventional family, learning to cook from library books. She also looks back on her teenage years as a music journalist, touring with the likes of Radiohead and the Beastie Boys, her early experiences of fame and the making of How to Be a Woman. item.title: ‘I said no thanks to the casting couch. But other actresses had problems’: Jane Alexander on 50 years of stardom
item.description: The Great White Hope, All the President’s Men, Kramer vs Kramer … Alexander has a CV most actors can only dream of. She talks us through the highs and lows – including a ‘beautiful’ encounter with Muhammad Ali Jane Alexander will never forget the play that won her a Tony award, a husband and her first film role. The Great White Hope, which ran on Broadway from 1968 to 1970, was based on the life of Black boxer Jack Johnson, who in 1908 became world heavyweight champion in segregated America. Alexander played Eleanor, a white woman married to an African American boxer also called Jack, at a time when interracial marriages were still illegal in many states. Decades later, when the play opened, the US supreme court had only recently struck down all remaining bans – and Alexander received hate mail and death threats for the role. Continue reading...

item.title: Will Hajime Moriyasu get a high-profile job in Europe after his eight years in charge of Japan?
item.description: The coach will leave early after the postponement of the Asian Cup and, while there has been clear progress, some had hoped for better results at World Cups A popular Christmas tradition in Japan is to head to KFC but there is an unexpected item on the menu to chew over this year for the millions who do so – a meaty debate over Hajime Moriyasu’s eight years as national-team head coach. Among the many consequences of the Asian Cup’s postponement from January 2027 to December is the fact his tenure has ended early. The 58-year-old was supposed to stay on until February to cap that lengthy spell with (hopefully) a deserved trophy, hand over to Go Oiwa and then, perhaps, blaze a trail to Europe. Instead he left this month, after 113 games in charge during which Japan became a global force to be reckoned with, even if there are those who think he underdelivered. Continue reading...

Pinto disappeared from her home in east London a couple of weeks ago and has so far defied the forecasts of tarot readings and the “witchy ladies” predicting his return. item.title: AI's shock-and-awe raid on maths looks like pride before a fall | Rafael Behr
item.description: Machines are bulldozing through hard problems to assert the power of their tech bro creators, not to advance human knowledge In most walks of life, trying something 12,363,153,437,138 times and getting the same result is reason enough to assume it works every time. Not in maths, where a conjecture that holds up more than 12tn times looks very probably true but doesn’t qualify as proven. That was the status of the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous mathematical conundrums in existence, until last week . Then Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working at Anthropic, said he and his collaborator, Claude AI, had crossed the line from conjecture to proof. Early one Saturday morning when she was eight years old, Araújo and her father were playing soccer in Golden Gate Park, near their home in San Francisco, when they heard a woman scream. Her father, a former Olympic runner for Brazil, told her to stay and bolted to help; Araújo, scared and alone, ran after him, and instead found the woman in a clearing, naked from the waist down. Araújo was too young to understand what had happened, but she knew something was wrong. But it is an unexpectedly intimate, emotional piece of work, a big-hearted odd-couple story, which is perhaps slightly more complex than at first appears. Emma Fogarty is a smart, garrulous woman from Abbeyleix in County Laois in the Republic of Ireland who has EB: epidermolysis bullosa, a rare condition which means that her skin is permanently, agonisingly painful and requires a daily calvary of bandaging and re-bandaging. item.title: Sali Hughes on beauty: lactonic scents will have you smelling like cream soda – in a good way
item.description: These fragrances are on trend right now, and smelling creamy can, it turns out, be surprisingly pleasant When the fragrance world picks a theme, it goes in hard. In the space of one month, I had close to a dozen new “lactonic” (that is, milky or creamy themed) perfumes to try. Instinctively, I wasn’t keen – I haven’t touched a glass of milk since nursery school – and so I eased myself in with DedCool’s Mocha Magic (£24 for 15ml), which adds a shot of coffee to the brand’s Xtra Milk fragrance that I love. This is immediately creamy, rich and bittersweet, like tiramisu, right down to that same dry hit of cocoa powder at the back of the throat. As in life, the coffee wears off, but the vanilla, spice and woody notes hang around for an impressively long spell. As with almost everything right now, it’s sweet, but not overbearingly so. item.title: ‘Half price!’ ‘Only two left!’ How to resist the bargains you just don’t need – this Black Friday and beyond
item.description: Everywhere you look, there’s another unrepeatable deal at an unmissable price. What’s on offer will make you happier, smarter and sexier. Except, of course, it won’t. Let us help you ignore the ‘consumption noise’ The other morning a parcel arrived and I was momentarily mystified by its contents. Peering at what appeared to be a shiny maroon and pink cushion cover, the penny eventually dropped. It was the fancy “Sweat Bag” I had bought on impulse when it popped up on Instagram after a particularly trying day. The blurb had convinced me it was the perfect solution for storing sweaty gym gear, ensuring that everything else in my bag remained pristine. “Whether it’s a 6am class before work or squeezing in lunchtime workouts, the Sweat Bag moves with you, wherever your day takes you.” I liked the idea of being this busy, efficient human, but in reality, I generally head straight home after my workouts and collapse beside the nearest biscuit tin. I had no business spending, ahem, £39 on it.

Science fiction is forever asking what it means to be human and, in the future dystopia first painted by Ridley Scott’s 1982 movie, the answer is that we are what we remember: we are the experiences we preserve as a collection of short films inside our heads. item.title: The story of how Pelé and Maradona went from friends to bitter rivals
item.description: A new book charts the complicated relationship between the two legends, starting on a sunny afternoon in Rio in 1979 Pelé and Diego Maradona first met in April 1979, not long after the Argentinian led his country’s under-20 side to the finals of the World Youth Cup. Maradona told a journalist friend that his dream was to meet the Brazilian, and after a few weeks of aborted attempts to bring them together – mostly because Diego did not want to travel on a Monday, the one day he had free for his girlfriend Claudia – the meeting finally took place in Rio. Reporter Guillermo Blanco, who was writing about the meeting for Argentinian sports magazine El Gráfico, got the OK from Pelé’s people and was so intent on making it happen that he checked Maradona onto a flight one Sunday night without telling him. He collared the young man after Argentine Juniors played Huracán and then raced to the airport and put him on a plane with his father, his agent and a photographer. Continue reading...

item.description: Don’t take the bait offered up by ‘conservation’ charities. Fishing is about as good for our ecosystems as tobacco is for our health Drumroll please. I am about to unveil the species of fish that’s best to eat if you want to protect the living seas. Ta-dah! It’s … I hope that clears things up. Unfortunately, over the past few years, a noisy industry has developed to tell you otherwise. You’re doing the planet a favour if you eat mackerel , sorry, cod, I mean haddock, no coley, make that pollack – oh, whoops! These choices might make you feel better about yourself. But they do nothing but harm to marine wildlife. The fish you should choose is none of the above. Cause, could I introduce you to effect? From 1 December, my neighbours take turns decorating their windows with that day’s number and festive lights, sometimes serving chocolate, cocoa or mulled wine in their front gardens. item.title: Secrets by Bob Woodward review – the world’s most famous reporter reveals all
item.description: The journalist who helped bring down Nixon on false starts, Watergate, and the art of cultivating a source ‘I have always disliked the term ‘investigative reporter’.” So writes Bob Woodward, one of the most celebrated reporters of our time – the man whose Watergate reporting with Carl Bernstein undoubtedly changed the US presidency and journalism itself for ever. His longtime boss, the Washington Post editor Ben Bradlee, disliked the term too: “All reporting is investigative,” Bradlee would say. The term conjures a certain sophistication, perhaps, but part of the beauty of a reporter’s work is how deceptively unsophisticated it can be. Secrets is a far-ranging, revealing memoir of an extraordinary career, but more than that, it is an ode to grinding it out – knocking on doors, asking and asking again, listening, taking notes, making notes on the notes, patiently following every lead to exhaustion. item.title: ‘I was physically beating myself up before a take’: Rory Culkin on anxiety, fatherhood and his famous brothers
item.description: The star of Lords of Chaos, Scream 4 and Gabriel was always drawn to the dark side. Is that why he seems happier in Hollywood than his better-known brothers – and why he loved making Nocturne with Stephen Graham? Rory Culkin is enjoying the autumn afternoon in a Manhattan park. The trees are a dazzling blur of yellows, greens, oranges and reds; the background silence is so pure you can hear it. “I’m here with my baby daughter, Havoc,” he says. “Havoc Moon.” I tell him that is the spookiest name ever. “Thank you,” he says. Culkin chuckles like a revving moped, his huge blue eyes lighting up. “Yes, it’s a weird one. I think she’ll probably be the opposite. A sweet, quiet girl. She’ll play a harp or something.” He explains its origin. “I just threw out names to my partner one night when we went to dinner. She wasn’t taking to anything. I then suggested Havoc, and she really liked it. She came up with the Moon part. When we got home there was fresh graffiti on the wall across the street sa

item.title: ‘Working with Kanye West? Talk about intractable egos!’ Caroline Shaw: the Pulitzer-winning composer everyone wants to work with
item.description: She has collaborated with classical giants such as Anne Sofie von Otter – and pop stars including Phoebe Bridgers. But what happened when Caroline Shaw hit ‘peak hamster wheel’? ‘Look at those!” gasps Caroline Shaw, standing next to me at an old steelworks in Germany’s industrial heartlands. Behind us are defunct concrete cooling towers and, in front, main buildings that sprawl off in a mix of brick and corrugated iron. But Shaw is looking upwards, awed by massive exhaust pipes looming overhead. This place, in the city of Bochum in western Germany, oozes post-industrial chic. These days it’s the Jahrhunderthalle , an arts venue where Shaw is performing later with the Attacca Quartet. For now the complex is shut, so we chat on a concrete bench. Intercepting Shaw, the youngest ever winner of the Pulitzer prize for music, is no mean feat: “in demand” is an understatement for this Portland-based US composer, singer, producer, violinist and viola player. item.title: Sustainable cement production via a liquid-phase pathway
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11313-w Sustainable cement production can be achieved by accelerating its reaction kinetics through a microwave carbon-plasma method, reducing the standard processing time from hours to seconds.

item.title: Context-dependent response of endothelial cells to PIK3CA mutation
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11318-5 Expression of PIK3CAH1047R in arterial precursors disrupts arterial differentiation and promotes the acquisition of venous features.

item.title: Augmenting reality with integrated photonics
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11146-7 Integrated photonics could overcome key size, power and performance trade-offs in augmented-reality glasses, enabling compact, efficient displays while opening opportunities across quantum computing, bioimaging and optical sensing.

item.title: Enzymatic living polymerization for polysaccharide synthesis
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11304-x An enzymatic method for making high-molecular-weight polysaccharides in a way similar to synthetic polymerization techniques, rather than biosynthetically, is presented.

item.title: Coherent parity oscillations in coupled minimal Kitaev chains
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11309-6 Coherent time-resolved rotations between parity states encoded by four poor man’s Majoranas are demonstrated in two coupled minimal Kitaev chains, providing a foundation for topologically protected qubits in longer chains.

item.title: Transcription from megabase-scale heterochromatin generates neural barcodes
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11311-y Interrogation of the clustered protocadherin locus shows an unexpected ability of genes to transcribe within a seemingly silent chromatin environment.

item.title: Structural basis of RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CAST systems
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11196-x Structural analyses reveal the mechanism underlying RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs) and provide a framework for developing CASTs into site-specific genome-editing tools.

item.title: Clinical landscape of cardiometabolic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11231-x This Review covers the current state of research into heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) from a variety of perspectives, focusing on the clinical context.

item.title: An extremophile transgene improves drought resistance and yield in cereals
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11151-w The use of an extremophile fungus-derived gene decouples the trade-off of drought stress and reduced crop yield by boosting drought resilience and increasing yields in wheat, rice and maize.

item.title: Disturbances and climate drive tree elevational shifts
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11354-1 Climate change and natural disturbances are key drivers of tree abundance dynamics: warming tends to shift tree abundance upslope whereas major disturbances, such as wildfires and insect outbreaks, tend to shift it downslope, creating opposing pressures on tree species’ elevational redistribution.

item.title: Unconventional resistivity reduction in NbP semimetal nanoribbons
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11288-8 Niobium phosphide semimetal nanoribbons show decreasing resistivity with decreasing width, unlike the classical behaviour of metals such as copper, offering a platform for nanoscale wires and interconnects via industry-friendly top-down nanofabrication.

item.title: De novo design of high-potency dual-target therapeutic peptides with ORIDTP
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11338-1 The artificial intelligence platform ORIDTP enabled de novo design of potent dual-target therapeutic peptides, generating candidate anti-obesity, antidiabetic and anticancer peptides with strong in vivo efficacy and broad cross-target generalizability.

item.title: Engineering signalling centres to trigger human trunk morphogenesis in vitro
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11326-5 A high-throughput synthetic embryology platform reveals how transient spatial cues establish two self-sustaining signalling centres that organize trunk-like morphogenesis, enabling the study of early human development and congenital disorders.

item.title: Rare-variant genetic architecture of height in over 1.4 million individuals
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11345-2 Analysis of exomes from over 1.4 million participants implicates 207 genes, including large effect coding variants and gene burden tests, and demonstrates the utility of large-scale sequencing for trait prediction and variant interpretation.

item.title: Submillimetre hot-electron transport in manganese-doped quantum dot solids
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11279-9 A phototransport regime driven by spin exchange is demonstrated in manganese-doped quantum dot solids, enabling the generation, long-range transport and regeneration of hot carriers and yielding submillimetre drift lengths.

item.title: Dortmund’s Beier halts Arsenal charge after thunderbolt from Gyökeres
item.description: Arsenal’s sky-high standards are slipping. For the second time in four days, Mikel Arteta’s side found themselves a goal up at half-time and apparently coasting toward victory, only for their opponents to rouse themselves and earn a deserved draw. After Newcastle on Saturday , this time it was an impressive Borussia Dortmund who became only the second side to take points off Arsenal in their past 15 group stage games in this competition. It could have been worse had an offside flag not ruled out Jobe ­Bellingham’s goal after Max Beier equalised a thunderbolt from Viktor Gyökeres. But the much-maligned Sweden striker was guilty of a glaring miss late on as Arsenal laid siege to Dortmund’s goal, racking up 30 shots by the final whistle. The German side had to hang on for a result that gave their travelling fans a night to remember, although Arteta admitted his players must be more clinical when Real Madrid and Jude Bellingham visit north London in a fortnight. item.title: Why I love Rome in winter: ‘We reclaim the city and slip back into familiar routines’
item.description: There is plenty of sunshine, the tourists have thinned out – and no one does a traditional Christmas like the Romans There was a time when, during a Rome winter, I would crave the warmer months. Not any more. The combination of intense heat and overtourism has made summer poco piacevole , as Italians would say – not very pleasant. So come mid-September, when the temperature drops and the crowds thin out, our mood lifts as we reclaim the city and slip back into familiar routines. In winter, the temperature is mostly mild and there is still plenty of sunshine (we do tend to grumble if the rain and grey skies persist for a few days). Rome is best seen on foot, and my favourite time to walk it is on a Sunday. Until earlier this year, I lived in Esquilino, a vibrant neighbourhood close to Termini train station. item.title: The Song of Stork and Dromedary by Anjet Daanje review – don’t miss this glorious epic inspired by Emily Brontë
item.description: The afterlife of a Yorkshire village girl who becomes a gothic literary icon is explored across three centuries, in a thrilling paean to the power of books I had a plan. I was going to nibble away at this great wedge of a book, a morsel a night, like a little reading mouse. But then the story swallowed me whole. I read Dutch author Anjet Daanje’s The Song of Stork and Dromedary over three feverish nights, and spent the days in between longing for the dark. This 720-page novel should come with a warning label: may cause severe infatuation. We begin in the fictional Yorkshire village of Bridge Fowling with Susan Knowles-Chester, a woman who attends to the dead. The year is 1847, and Susan knows the old ways, the threshold rituals: how to arrange a corpse so it doesn’t gape and gawp at the living. “The villagers have a horror of her work, for wherever she goes, she leaves grief like driftwood in her wake, yet when the time comes, many ask for her help, it is an open secret.” Continue read

Short of forgetting to put on his washable virgin wool navy trousers before striding towards the visitors’ dugout at Anfield, it’s difficult to imagine how Mauricio Pochettino’s spell in charge of Manchester United could have got off to a more humiliating start. Having witnessed his new team go a man and two goals down in less time than it takes to listen to Led Zeppelin’s Stairway to Heaven twice, it was a rendition of Sacked In The Morning that could be heard from the home fans inside 15 minutes. item.title: A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along

item.title: The Guide #270: Grand Theft Auto VI is everywhere – but is it really the cultural event of the decade?

Thousands upon thousands of days of leave booked and sick days taken to play the thing, costing the US economy an estimated $1bn (yep, another billion figure) in lost productivity. The scale of Grand Theft Auto VI – and the tidal wave of facts and figures surrounding its making and economic impact – truly boggles the mind. Raised in Bozeman, Montana, he was the founder and lead singer of the cult shoegaze-adjacent six-piece Strange Ranger, who left heartbroken a small, fervent fanbase when they announced their breakup in 2023. item.title: Danny Kelly loved football and never forgot the absurdity of earning a living talking about it | Max Rushden
item.description: The journalist and broadcaster who died last week aged 69 knew the enduring power of radio, even as the landscape changed so quickly It’s injury time at the Emirates on 29 October 2008, Arsenal are 4-3 up against Tottenham. Tom Huddlestone cushions a ball to Luka Modric, whose strike takes a deflection. It loops over Manuel Almunia and off a post into the path of Aaron Lennon, who prods it home and starts skipping towards the Spurs supporters before diving on to the ground and being enveloped by Modric, Benoît Assou-Ekotto, Darren Bent and a couple of pitch-invading fans. Pandemonium, for once, seems the apt way to describe it. But the real entertainment is happening in a radio studio at 18 Hatfields, London SE1; the old home of TalkSport. As the goal goes in, a guttural voice makes an indecipherable but very loud noise. It’s hard to transcribe – perhaps “ERRRRRAAAARRRGGHH”, or maybe “OOEEERRAAGGH”. In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. Flora told an audience at the London film festival premiere of the film that she played her best card then and showed Lineker an image of Maradona with Queen in 1981, during the band’s tour of Argentina. Maradona wearing a union jack T-shirt and Freddie Mercury an Argentina strip. It worked. Lineker said yes. item.description: The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature . My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career. After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. item.title: Sign up for the Moving the Goalposts newsletter: our free women’s football email
item.description: Get our roundup of women’s football for free twice a week, featuring the insights of experts such as Ada Hegerberg and Magdalena Eriksson Join us as we delve deeper into the wonderful world of women’s football in our weekly newsletter. It is informative, entertaining, global, critical – when needed – and, above all, passionate. Written mainly by Júlia Belas Trindade and Sophie Downey , expect guest appearances from stars such as Anita Asante, Ada Hegerberg and many more. Try our other sports emails: as well as the occasionally funny football email The Fiver from Monday to Friday, there are weekly catch-ups for cricket in The Spin and rugby union in The Breakdown , and our seven-day roundup of the best of our sports journalism in The Recap . Living in Australia? Try the Guardian Australia’s daily sports newsletter Continue reading...

item.title: Sign up for the Recap newsletter: our free sport highlights email
item.description: The best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s action Subscribe to get our editors’ pick of the Guardian’s award-winning sport coverage. We’ll email you the stand-out features and interviews, insightful analysis and highlights from the archive, plus films, podcasts, galleries and more – all arriving in your inbox at every Friday lunchtime. And we’ll set you up for the weekend and let you know our live coverage plans so you’ll be ahead of the game. Here’s what you can expect from us. Try our other sports emails: there’s daily football news and gossip in The Fiver , and weekly catch-ups for cricket in The Spin and rugby union in The Breakdown . Living in Australia?
